Pale yellow precipitate with AgNO3 suggests AgCl (white) but pale yellow could be AgI? Actually AgI is yellow, AgCl is white, AgBr is pale yellow. So pale yellow suggests AgBr. So presence of bromide? But we are testing chloride; but we see pale yellow precipitate, indicating maybe bromide present. However test is for chloride; if chloride present, precipitate would be white. So likely no chloride, maybe bromide or iodide. But we only need chloride test result: precipitate not white => no chloride. So we can note chloride negative.

Now hydroxide test: add KOH (maybe 6M) to sample, observe precipitate.

No precipitate with strong base suggests cation does not form insoluble hydroxide (e.g., not Fe3+, Al3+, Cr3+, etc). Could be alkali metal, alkaline earth (some form precipitates? Ca(OH)2 is slightly soluble, may not precipitate). So cation likely from group 1 (Na+, K+, Li+, etc) or maybe NH4+ (ammonium) which also doesn't precipitate with OH- (forms NH4OH). Also could be Ag+ (forms AgOH which decomposes to Ag2O precipitate? Might see precipitate). So likely not transition metal.

Now we have colorless, no flame color, no chloride, no hydroxide precipitate. So possible cations: alkali metals (Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, Cs+), ammonium (NH4+), maybe some heavy metal that gives no flame color and no precipitate with OH- like Tl+? But Tl+ gives flame? Not sure. Also maybe Ag+ but would give precipitate with AgNO3? Actually adding AgNO3 to sample gave pale yellow precipitate, which could be AgBr if Br- present, but that would be from anion not cation. So cation could be Ag+? But Ag+ with AgNO3 would not precipitate (since same ion). So precipitate came from anion reacting with Ag+. So cation could be anything.
